questions.question:
Consider the following road network where the distances for each pair $(i, j)$ of cities are shown. Formulate the problem mathematically, where the shortest path from city $s$ to city $t$ has to be found.
Convert your mathematical model into the mathematical form of the Minimum Cost Network Flow problem. Specifically mention the assumptions needed.
questions.modelAnswer:
Arcs and distances $c_{ij}$: $(s,1) = 5$, $(s,2) = 4$, $(2,1) = 2$, $(1,3) = 6$, $(2,4) = 3$, $(3,4) = 3$, $(3,t) = 4$, $(4,t) = 8$.
Variables: $x_{ij} = 1$ if arc $(i,j)$ is on the path, 0 otherwise.
Shortest path ILP:
$$\min\ 5x_{s1} + 4x_{s2} + 2x_{21} + 6x_{13} + 3x_{24} + 3x_{34} + 4x_{3t} + 8x_{4t}$$
subject to (out minus in at each node)
$$s:\ x_{s1} + x_{s2} = 1$$
$$1:\ x_{13} - x_{s1} - x_{21} = 0, \qquad 2:\ x_{21} + x_{24} - x_{s2} = 0$$
$$3:\ x_{34} + x_{3t} - x_{13} = 0, \qquad 4:\ x_{4t} - x_{24} - x_{34} = 0$$
$$t:\ -x_{3t} - x_{4t} = -1, \qquad x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}.$$
Minimum cost network flow form:
$$\min \sum_{(i,j)} c_{ij}x_{ij} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_j x_{ij} - \sum_j x_{ji} = b_i \ \ \forall i, \qquad 0 \le x_{ij} \le u_{ij}$$
with $b_s = 1$ (supply of one unit), $b_t = -1$ (demand of one unit), $b_1 = b_2 = b_3 = b_4 = 0$ (transshipment nodes), costs $c_{ij}$ = distances and capacities $u_{ij} = 1$.
Assumptions: one unit of flow is sent from $s$ to $t$; total supply equals total demand ($\sum_i b_i = 0$); costs are non-negative (no negative cycles); arc capacities are 1 (or at least 1). The binary condition can then be relaxed to $0 \le x_{ij} \le 1$ because the min-cost flow LP has integer optimal solutions, so the flow picks out a path.
Not asked, but useful: the shortest distance is 15, along $s \to 1 \to 3 \to t$ ($5 + 6 + 4$) or $s \to 2 \to 4 \to t$ ($4 + 3 + 8$).

rubric.point: Objective: total distance $\sum c_{ij}x_{ij}$ with the network's distances
Flow constraints: +1 out of $s$, −1 at $t$, 0 at nodes 1–4 (written for this network)
Min-cost flow form $\sum_j x_{ij} - \sum_j x_{ji} = b_i$, $0 \le x_{ij} \le u_{ij}$
Assumptions stated: one unit of flow, supply = demand, non-negative costs, integral LP so 0/1 flows

questions.question:
Consider the set of items $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$ that you want to invest your R1000 into. Individual profits that can be earned are R50, R100, R250, R20 and R90. The joint profits pairwise are as follows:
$$P_{12} = 10, \quad P_{13} = 20, \quad P_{14} = 5, \quad P_{15} = 6,$$
$$P_{21} = 3, \quad P_{23} = 7, \quad P_{24} = 6, \quad P_{25} = 2,$$
$$P_{31} = 10, \quad P_{32} = 15, \quad P_{34} = 20, \quad P_{35} = 1,$$
$$P_{41} = 12, \quad P_{42} = 3, \quad P_{43} = 7, \quad P_{45} = 6,$$
$$P_{51} = 6, \quad P_{52} = 10, \quad P_{53} = 1, \quad P_{54} = 2.$$
The cost of each are:
$$c_1 = 200, \quad c_2 = 500, \quad c_3 = 400, \quad c_4 = 50, \quad c_5 = 600.$$
Formulate the problem mathematically and write in the compacted form as:
$$f(x) = b^\top x + \frac{1}{2}x^\top Mx,$$
where $x \in \mathbb{R}^5$ is your decision variable, $b \in \mathbb{R}^5$ is a constant vector and $M$ is a symmetric but constant matrix. Show that the function can be written as $f(x) = \frac{1}{2}x^\top \tilde{M}x$, where $\tilde{M}$ is a symmetric but constant matrix.
questions.modelAnswer:
Variables: $x_i = 1$ if we invest in item $i$, 0 otherwise.
Model (quadratic knapsack):
$$\max\ f(x) = 50x_1 + 100x_2 + 250x_3 + 20x_4 + 90x_5 + \sum_{i=1}^{5}\sum_{j \ne i} P_{ij}x_ix_j$$
$$\text{s.t.}\quad 200x_1 + 500x_2 + 400x_3 + 50x_4 + 600x_5 \le 1000, \qquad x_i \in \{0, 1\}.$$
Compact form: $b = (50, 100, 250, 20, 90)^\top$. The pair $\{i, j\}$ earns $P_{ij} + P_{ji}$ when both are chosen, so take $M_{ij} = M_{ji} = P_{ij} + P_{ji}$ for $i \ne j$ and $M_{ii} = 0$. Then $\tfrac12 x^\top Mx = \tfrac12\sum_{i \ne j} M_{ij}x_ix_j = \sum_{i<j}(P_{ij} + P_{ji})x_ix_j = \sum_{i \ne j}P_{ij}x_ix_j$, which is exactly the joint-profit term:
$$M = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 13 & 30 & 17 & 12 \\ 13 & 0 & 22 & 9 & 12 \\ 30 & 22 & 0 & 27 & 2 \\ 17 & 9 & 27 & 0 & 8 \\ 12 & 12 & 2 & 8 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad f(x) = b^\top x + \tfrac12 x^\top Mx.$$
$M$ is symmetric and constant.
Pure quadratic form: since $x_i \in \{0,1\}$, $x_i^2 = x_i$, so $b^\top x = \sum_i b_ix_i^2 = \tfrac12 x^\top(2\,\text{diag}(b))x$. Hence
$$f(x) = \tfrac12 x^\top \tilde{M}x, \qquad \tilde{M} = M + 2\,\text{diag}(b) = \begin{pmatrix} 100 & 13 & 30 & 17 & 12 \\ 13 & 200 & 22 & 9 & 12 \\ 30 & 22 & 500 & 27 & 2 \\ 17 & 9 & 27 & 40 & 8 \\ 12 & 12 & 2 & 8 & 180 \end{pmatrix},$$
which is symmetric (a symmetric $M$ plus a diagonal matrix) and constant.
Not asked, but a check: the best affordable choice is items 2, 3, 4 (cost 950), profit $100 + 250 + 20$ (single items) $+ 22 + 9 + 27$ (pairs 2–3, 2–4, 3–4) $= 428$.

rubric.point: Objective: individual profits plus pairwise profits $P_{ij}x_ix_j$
$M_{ij} = P_{ij} + P_{ji}$ ($i \ne j$), $M_{ii} = 0$, with the reason (each pair counted twice, halved by ½)
Uses $x_i^2 = x_i$ to write $b^\top x = \tfrac12 x^\top 2\,\text{diag}(b)\,x$
